Hatchlings emerge at a remarkably modest weight, with neonatal body mass averaging just 7.5 grams [Wwb = 7.5 grams] immediately after emergence from the shell. This low birth mass reflects the altricial condition typical of the genus, as newly hatched chicks are sparsely covered in white down and entirely dependent on parental brooding. Within the first few days post-hatching, the nestlings undergo a rapid phase of mass gain, and the initial wet weight of freshly laid eggs has been recorded at 10.3 grams [Ww0 = 10.3 grams], indicating that the egg itself constitutes a substantial maternal investment relative to the hatchling’s size. By the end of the third week, these developing chicks are capable of short flights and begin to perch at the cavity entrance, though they continue to receive prey from adults for several more days. The rate of mass gain during this interval is steep, with chicks consuming large quantities of noctuid moths and beetles brought at frequent intervals by the provisioning adults.

The adult body mass fluctuates seasonally, with individuals reaching their peak weight in late autumn when fat reserves are deposited to endure the winter months, followed by a decline during the energetically demanding breeding season when both parents engage in intensive provisioning of altricial nestlings.
